# Brazilian public datasets {#sec-m2-bases}

This chapter is what makes R particularly productive for the Ministry's work: instead of
browsing portals, downloading ZIPs and opening shapefiles one by one, the main Brazilian
datasets come through functions: versioned, documented and with the IBGE code as the key.

```{r}
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

# default basemap for mapview(): OpenStreetMap
mapview::mapviewOptions(basemaps = c("OpenStreetMap", "Esri.WorldGrayCanvas", "Esri.WorldImagery"))
```

## `geobr`: official IBGE boundaries and geometries

Documentation and examples: <https://ipeagit.github.io/geobr/>.

```{r}
#| eval: false
geobr::list_geobr()   # every function, with the available years
```

The ones we use most:

| Function | What it returns |
|:--|:--|
| `read_country()`, `read_region()`, `read_state()` | national, regional and state boundaries |
| `read_municipality()` | municipal boundaries |
| `read_census_tract()` | census tracts |
| `read_weighting_area()` | weighting areas |
| `read_statistical_grid()` | IBGE statistical grid |
| `read_urban_area()` | urbanised areas |
| `read_health_facilities()` | health facilities (CNES) |
| `read_schools()` | schools (School Census) |
| `read_biomes()`, `read_conservation_units()`, `read_indigenous_land()` | environmental and territorial boundaries |

```{r}
arquivo <- "dados/brutos/muni_br.gpkg"

if (!file.exists(arquivo)) {
  br <- geobr::read_municipality(code_muni = "all", year = 2022,
                                 simplified = TRUE, showProgress = FALSE)
  sf::st_write(br, arquivo, quiet = TRUE)
}
br <- sf::st_read(arquivo, quiet = TRUE)

nrow(br)
head(br, 3) |> sf::st_drop_geometry()
```

Arguments that matter:

- `code_muni` / `code_state`: accepts an IBGE code, a state abbreviation (`"PR"`) or `"all"`.
- `year`: the boundaries change with each census and each new municipality. **Always state it**.
- `simplified = TRUE` (default): lightweight geometry, for maps. Use `FALSE` to measure area.
- `cache = TRUE` (default): the file is stored locally after the first *download*.
- `output`: the type of object returned. The default, `"sf"`, loads everything into memory; see below
  the alternative for large datasets.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Large datasets: `output = "duckdb"`

Census tracts, the statistical grid or the unsimplified municipal boundaries weigh hundreds
of MB, and spatial operations on them become slow in `sf`. In those cases, ask `geobr`
for a **DuckDB** table, with `output = "duckdb"`. It is not loaded into memory: `geobr`
returns a "lazy" table from the `duckspatial` package, and filters and spatial operations
run in the database. Only the result comes back to R, as an ordinary `sf` object, at `collect()`.

```{r}
#| eval: false
mun <- geobr::read_municipality(code_muni = "all", year = 2022, output = "duckdb")

mun |>
  dplyr::filter(abbrev_state == "PR") |>
  duckspatial::ddbs_transform("EPSG:5880") |>          # metric projection, as in sf
  duckspatial::ddbs_area(new_column = "area_m2") |>
  dplyr::collect()                                     # only here do the data come into R
```

`duckspatial` is introduced in the DuckDB chapter (@sec-m3-duckdb). For the course examples,
`sf` is enough; `duckspatial` makes a difference when the dataset does not fit comfortably in memory.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Don't know the municipality's IBGE code by heart? Look it up in the boundaries

The boundaries we just read already contain the name and code of every municipality:

```{r}
br |>
  sf::st_drop_geometry() |>
  dplyr::filter(stringr::str_detect(name_muni, "Fortaleza")) |>
  dplyr::select(code_muni, name_muni, abbrev_state)
```

Notice that five municipalities came back, in four states: "Fortaleza" appears in the name of several. That is
why the name alone is not a key, and the IBGE code is. The other way round, from code to name:

```{r}
br |>
  sf::st_drop_geometry() |>
  dplyr::filter(code_muni == 4106902) |>
  dplyr::select(code_muni, name_muni, abbrev_state)
```

`geobr` also has `lookup_muni()`, which does the same search online, without needing
the boundaries:

```{r}
#| eval: false
geobr::lookup_muni(name_muni = "fortaleza", year = 2022)
geobr::lookup_muni(code_muni = 4106902, year = 2022)
```
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## The right boundaries for each use

For **maps**, `simplified = TRUE` is what you want: it renders fast and the difference is
invisible at print scale. To **measure area, intersect or compute population in a
catchment**, use `simplified = FALSE`. The simplified geometry cuts corners and
introduces an error of a few per cent, besides leaving gaps between neighbouring polygons.
:::

## `censobr`: Census microdata and aggregates

Documentation: <https://ipeagit.github.io/censobr/>. `censobr` distributes the Census in
Parquet format, with lazy reading: the function returns an `arrow` object that is only materialised at
`collect()`. This makes it possible to work with the whole Census on an ordinary laptop.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# aggregates by census tract
setores <- censobr::read_tracts(year = 2022, dataset = "Basico",
                                as_data_frame = FALSE, showProgress = FALSE)

pop_setor <- setores |>
  dplyr::filter(abbrev_state == "PR") |>
  dplyr::select(code_tract, code_muni, name_muni, V0001) |>   # V0001 = resident population
  dplyr::collect()
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
# population and household microdata
censobr::read_population(year = 2010, columns = c("code_muni", "V0601", "V6036"))
censobr::read_households(year = 2010, columns = c("code_muni", "V0201"))

# variable dictionary: essential, the names are codes
censobr::data_dictionary(year = 2022, dataset = "tracts")
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## `add_labels`: translates the codes of categorical variables

Since a recent update, `read_population()` and `read_households()` accept
`add_labels = "pt"`, which replaces each categorical variable's raw code with its label
(in Portuguese), directly when reading, without having to join with `data_dictionary()` by hand:

```{r}
#| eval: false
censobr::read_population(year = 2010, columns = c("code_muni", "V0601", "V6036"),
                         add_labels = "pt")
```

Check the installed version with `packageVersion("censobr")`: this material assumes `>= 0.6.0`,
which is when `add_labels` was introduced.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## About the available years

`censobr` covers 2000, 2010 and, in the latest versions, the 2022 Census, which was released
gradually. If `year = 2022` is not available in your version, switch to `2010`: the
code is identical, only the variable names change. Check with
`packageVersion("censobr")` and `censobr::data_dictionary()`.
:::

Matching `censobr` (attributes) and `geobr` (geometry) is done through the tract or
municipality code: module 1's `join`, now with geometry on one side.

```{r}
#| eval: false
setores_geo <- geobr::read_census_tract(code_tract = "PR", year = 2022,
                                        simplified = FALSE, showProgress = FALSE)

setores_pop <- setores_geo |>
  dplyr::left_join(pop_setor, by = "code_tract", relationship = "one-to-one")
```

## `sidrar`: SIDRA/IBGE tables

Documentation: <https://cran.r-project.org/package=sidrar>. SIDRA is where the aggregate
series live: population estimates, projections, municipal GDP, PNAD, agricultural output. `sidrar`
fetches any table by its number.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Resident population by municipality (2022 Census, table 4709)
pop <- sidrar::get_sidra(
  x = 4709,
  variable = 93,
  geo = "City",
  geo.filter = list("State" = 41)    # 41 = Paraná
)

# Municipal GDP (table 5938)
pib <- sidrar::get_sidra(x = 5938, variable = 37, period = "2021",
                         geo = "City", geo.filter = list("State" = 41))

# search for tables and look at the structure of one of them
sidrar::search_sidra("população")
sidrar::info_sidra(4709)
```

The output comes "wide" and with long column names in Portuguese. It is a classic case for
`janitor::clean_names()` and for module 1's `pivot_longer`.

```{r}
#| eval: false
pop_limpa <- pop |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    code_muni = as.numeric(municipio_codigo),
    municipio = municipio,
    populacao = valor
  )
```

::: {.callout-tip}
SIDRA limits the size of a query. For long series for every municipality in Brazil,
split by state in a loop (`lapply` over state codes) and stack with `bind_rows()`. It is the pattern from
module 1.
:::

## `osmdata` and `osmextract`: OpenStreetMap

Documentation: <https://docs.ropensci.org/osmdata/> and <https://docs.ropensci.org/osmextract/>.
Two routes, for different needs:

- **`osmdata`** queries the Overpass API live. Ideal for small areas and specific
  features (petrol stations, terminals, one highway).
- **`osmextract`** downloads ready-made regional extracts as `.pbf` (Geofabrik). Ideal for whole
  road networks and for feeding `r5r` in module 4.

```{r}
arquivo_br116 <- "dados/brutos/br116_serra.gpkg"

if (!file.exists(arquivo_br116)) {
  consulta <- osmdata::opq(bbox = c(-49.40, -25.75, -48.40, -25.15), timeout = 120) |>
    osmdata::add_osm_feature(key = "ref", value = "BR-116") |>
    osmdata::osmdata_sf()

  br116 <- consulta$osm_lines |>
    dplyr::select(dplyr::any_of(c("osm_id", "name", "ref", "highway", "lanes", "maxspeed"))) |>
    sf::st_transform(4674)

  sf::st_write(br116, arquivo_br116, quiet = TRUE)
}

br116 <- sf::st_read(arquivo_br116, quiet = TRUE)
nrow(br116)
sf::st_geometry_type(br116, by_geometry = FALSE) |> unique()
```

OSM does not clip the geometry to the query's `bbox`, so it is worth checking visually whether the
returned segments really fall in the area of interest:

```{r}
mapview::mapview(br116)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-br116
#| fig-cap: "Segments of the BR-116 in the Serra do Mar area, according to OpenStreetMap"
#| fig-height: 4.4
arquivo <- "dados/brutos/muni_pr_sc.gpkg"
muni <- sf::st_read(arquivo, quiet = TRUE)

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = muni, fill = "grey97", colour = "grey85", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_sf(data = br116, colour = "#e07b39", linewidth = 0.7) +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(-49.45, -48.35), ylim = c(-25.80, -25.10)) +
  labs(caption = "Source: OpenStreetMap.") +
  theme_void(base_size = 10)
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
# osmextract: the road network of a whole state, from the .pbf
rede <- osmextract::oe_get(
  place = "Ceará",
  layer = "lines",
  query = "SELECT osm_id, highway, name FROM lines WHERE highway IS NOT NULL",
  download_directory = "dados/brutos/osm"
)

# only the .pbf file, which is what r5r consumes (module 4)
osmextract::oe_download(
  file_url = osmextract::oe_match("Ceará")$url,
  download_directory = "dados/brutos/osm"
)
```

::: {.callout-important}
## OSM is excellent, with two caveats

1. **It is collaborative.** The geometry is usually very good; the attributes (`maxspeed`, `lanes`,
   `surface`) are incomplete and vary by region. For the official alignment of federal
   highways, the source is **DNIT's SNV** (<http://servicos.dnit.gov.br/vgeo/>) or the
   [Ministry of Transport's georeferenced database](https://www.gov.br/transportes/pt-br/assuntos/transporte-terrestre/base-de-dados-georreferenciada).
2. **It changes every day.** Record the extraction date: `dados/brutos/br116_serra.gpkg` with the date
   in the name is a practice that saves the report's reproducibility.
:::

## Other sources worth knowing

| Source | How to access | Use |
|:--|:--|:--|
| SNV: federal highways | [VGeo/DNIT](http://servicos.dnit.gov.br/vgeo/), manual *download* | official alignment, segments, jurisdiction |
| Ministry of Transport georeferenced database (BIT) | [Ministry portal](https://www.gov.br/transportes/pt-br/assuntos/dados-de-transportes/bit) | highways, railways, waterways, ports, airports |
| PNCT: traffic counts | [PNCT data](http://servicos.dnit.gov.br/dadospnct) | AADT per station, on the federal network |
| ANTAQ: Estatístico Aquaviário | [download](https://web3.antaq.gov.br/ea/sense/download.html) | cargo, berthing, facilities |
| Access to Opportunities (Ipea) | `aopdata` | accessibility and opportunities in 20 cities |
| Public transport GTFS | municipal portals, [Mobility Database](https://mobilitydatabase.org/feeds?q=brazil) | public transport network |
| Address geocoding | `geocodebr` | address → coordinate (module 3) |

In modules 3 and 4 we use `aopdata`, `geocodebr`, GTFS and the ANTAQ data; the first two
items of the table come into the next case study, as an official alternative to OSM.
